topic: multiple sclerosis

page.mentor_intro: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system characterized by multifocal demyelination, astrocytic gliosis, and axonal transection, manifesting as relapsing-remitting or progressive disease requiring early diagnostic McDonald criteria verification and disease-modifying treatment.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical disease phenotype is standardized by the Lublin classification into clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~85% of presentations), secondary progressive MS (SPMS), and primary progressive MS (PPMS, ~15%), each characterized by disease activity (clinical relapses or new MRI lesions) and progression.

ECTRIMS/EAN guidelines recommend starting disease-modifying therapy early in patients with CIS and abnormal baseline brain MRI showing >=2 demyelinating lesions, as early treatment significantly reduces conversion to clinically definite MS and delays long-term disability accumulation.

standard_knowledge.claim: According to the revised 2017 McDonald criteria, diagnosis requires objective clinical and neuroimaging demonstration of lesions disseminated in space (DIS, involving >=2 of 4 typical CNS regions) and time (DIT, simultaneous contrast-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions or new lesions on follow-up).

The 2017 McDonald criteria established that the presence of CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (unique bands present in CSF but absent in matched serum) substitutes for the requirement of dissemination in time in patients with typical clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) fulfilling DIS criteria.

uncertainties: Stopping disease-modifying therapies in stable older patients (>60 years) with non-active secondary progressive MS.
Long-term neuroprotective impact of Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors on smoldering non-active progression in progressive MS.
mcq_angles: CSF oligoclonal bands role in 2017 McDonald criteria: allows formal diagnosis of MS at initial presentation if DIS is met.
The 4 anatomical zones for Dissemination in Space: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord.
Definition of active secondary progressive MS: gradual disability worsening over >=6-12 months independent of relapses, but with superimposed relapses or new gadolinium-enhancing lesions.

topic: Multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapy

page.mentor_intro: Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) for multiple sclerosis have expanded into highly effective targeted immunomodulatory agents, including B-cell-depleting monoclonal antibodies, selective cell adhesion blockers, and oral pulsed immune reconstitution therapies that markedly reduce relapse rates and delay disability progression.

teaching_points.claim: In the AFFIRM trial, the alpha-4 integrin antagonist natalizumab reduced annualized relapse rates by 68% (p<0.001) and reduced sustained disability progression by 42%, though long-term therapy mandates strict anti-JCV antibody index surveillance to stratify progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) risk.

ECTRIMS/EAN consensus guidelines support early use of high-efficacy DMTs (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, natalizumab, alemtuzumab) in patients with highly active disease (frequent disabling relapses or multiple spinal/infratentorial gadolinium-enhancing lesions).

standard_knowledge.claim: In the twin OPERA I and OPERA II phase 3 trials, the humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody ocrelizumab significantly reduced annualized relapse rates by 46-47% (p<0.001) and reduced 12-week confirmed disability progression by 40% compared with subcutaneous interferon beta-1a in relapsing MS.

In the phase 3 ORATORIO trial, ocrelizumab became the first disease-modifying therapy to demonstrate efficacy in primary progressive MS, significantly reducing 12-week confirmed disability progression by 24% (p=0.03) and decreasing total brain volume loss compared to placebo.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term benefits of early intensive therapy versus rapid escalation in patients presenting with moderate baseline lesion loads.
Safety and rebound disease flare following discontinuation of natalizumab or S1P receptor modulators (fingolimod) prior to pregnancy.
mcq_angles: First DMT approved with proven disability reduction in primary progressive MS: ocrelizumab (ORATORIO trial).
Major safety concern with natalizumab: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus reactivation.

topic: Myasthenia gravis targeted immunotherapy

page.mentor_intro: Targeted immunotherapies for generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) have revolutionized management of acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive disease through selective terminal complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab, ravulizumab) and neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) blockade (efgartigimod), inducing rapid functional improvement in refractory disease.

teaching_points.claim: In the randomized phase 3 REGAIN trial by Howard and colleagues, the terminal complement C5 inhibitor eculizumab produced significant, clinically meaningful, and sustained improvements in Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) and QMG scores in refractory anti-AChR-positive generalized myasthenia gravis.

In the phase 3 ADAPT trial, the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) antagonist efgartigimod achieved rapid reductions in total IgG and anti-AChR antibody titers, producing significant, durable MG-ADL responder rates (67.7% vs 29.7% with placebo; p<0.0001) in generalized myasthenia gravis.

International consensus guidance mandates that all patients receiving terminal complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) must receive meningococcal vaccination (serogroups A, C, W, Y and B) at least 2 weeks prior to therapy and prophylactic oral antibiotics until immunization takes effect, due to an increased risk of invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection.

standard_knowledge.claim: The phase 3 CHAMPION-MG trial demonstrated that the long-acting terminal complement C5 inhibitor ravulizumab produced rapid and sustained improvements in MG-ADL scores through week 26 with convenient 8-weekly maintenance dosing.

uncertainties: Choosing between complement inhibitors versus FcRn antagonists in acute myasthenic crisis as an alternative to plasmapheresis or IVIG.
Long-term infection risk and hypogammaglobulinemia during cyclical repeat courses of FcRn inhibitors.
mcq_angles: Mechanism of efgartigimod: blocks the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), accelerating endogenous IgG and pathogenic autoantibody catabolism.
Mandatory safety requirement before initiating complement inhibitors (eculizumab/ravulizumab): vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis (MenACWY and MenB).
Specific indication for complement inhibitors: anti-AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis (complement is NOT activated in anti-MuSK MG, which is mediated by IgG4).
First-line treatment of choice for anti-MuSK positive myasthenia gravis: rituximab (anti-CD20).

topic: Mycobacterial and Fungal Arthritis

page.mentor_intro: Mycobacterial and fungal arthritis are chronic, indolent joint infections presenting as slowly progressive monoarticular arthritis, characteristically causing substantial diagnostic delay and requiring synovial tissue histopathology, acid-fast and fungal staining, mycobacterial culture/PCR, and prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy combined with surgical debridement.

teaching_points.claim: ATS/CDC/IDSA clinical guidelines recommend treating musculoskeletal and joint tuberculosis with standard four-drug therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for a total duration of 6 to 9 months.

standard_knowledge.claim: Tuberculous arthritis typically presents as an indolent, insidious, chronic monoarthritis (most commonly affecting weight-bearing joints: knee, hip, ankle) or spondylodiscitis (Pott's disease); synovial fluid smears are positive for acid-fast bacilli in <30% of cases, making synovial biopsy with granuloma identification and mycobacterial culture/PCR the diagnostic gold standard.
Candida arthritis is treated with surgical debridement or drainage plus fluconazole or an echinocandin for at least 6 weeks; infected prostheses require removal (often two-stage revision).

Endemic fungal joint infections (Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Sporothrix schenckii) occur via hematogenous dissemination or direct occupational inoculation (e.g., rose thorn prick causing sporotrichoid lymphocutaneous arthritis), treated with intravenous amphotericin B followed by prolonged oral itraconazole for 6-12 months.

uncertainties: Optimal timing and surgical indication for joint arthrodesis versus arthroplasty following microbiological cure of tuberculous joint destruction.
Utility of rapid synovial fluid GeneXpert MTB/RIF PCR in culture-negative chronic inflammatory monoarthritis.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic investigation of choice for suspected tuberculous arthritis: synovial biopsy (shows caseating granulomas and culture positivity far higher than synovial fluid aspiration).
Phemister triad on X-ray in tuberculous arthritis: periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, and gradual joint space narrowing.
Treatment duration for skeletal tuberculosis: 6 to 9 months of guideline-directed antituberculous chemotherapy.
Sporothrix schenckii classical presentation: nodular lymphangitis and subacute monoarthritis following rose-thorn puncture treated with itraconazole.

topic: Mycophenolate Mofetil versus Cyclophosphamide regimens

page.mentor_intro: In proliferative lupus nephritis (ISN/RPS Class III/IV), mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and intravenous cyclophosphamide achieve comparable remission induction efficacy, with MMF demonstrating superior tolerability, higher response rates in non-Caucasian populations, and established superiority as maintenance therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial established that a low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide induction regimen (six fortnightly pulses of 500 mg, cumulative dose 3 g) followed by azathioprine achieved long-term renal remission, renal function preservation, and 10-year survival equivalent to high-dose cyclical cyclophosphamide.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the ALMS induction trial, mycophenolate mofetil (target 3 g/day) was not superior to intravenous cyclophosphamide overall (renal response 56.2% versus 53.0%), with better responses in Black and Hispanic patients.

In the ALMS maintenance trial, Dooley and colleagues proved that MMF was significantly superior to azathioprine in maintaining renal remission (treatment failure rate 16.4% vs 32.4%; HR 0.44; p=0.003) and significantly prolonged time to renal flare over 36 months.

EULAR/ERA-EDTA guidelines recommend MMF or low-dose Euro-Lupus intravenous cyclophosphamide combined with glucocorticoids as preferred first-line induction for Class III/IV lupus nephritis, with cyclophosphamide preferred in patients with rapidly declining renal function or nephrotic-range proteinuria failing oral therapy.

uncertainties: Optimal triple immunosuppression regimens (MMF plus voclosporin or belimumab) as first-line therapy in high-risk proliferative lupus nephritis.
Fertility preservation protocols (GnRH agonists, oocyte cryopreservation) during pulse cyclophosphamide therapy in women of childbearing age.
mcq_angles: ALMS trial primary outcome: MMF is non-inferior to IV cyclophosphamide for induction and superior for maintenance compared to azathioprine.
Euro-Lupus regimen dosing: 500 mg IV cyclophosphamide every 2 weeks for a total of 6 doses (cumulative 3 g).
Toxicity differences: cyclophosphamide carries risks of premature ovarian failure, hemorrhagic cystitis, and bladder transitional cell carcinoma; MMF is teratogenic but preserves ovarian reserve.
Racial differences in ALMS induction: Black and Hispanic patients exhibited significantly higher response rates to MMF than cyclophosphamide.

topic: Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome

page.mentor_intro: Mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS) are cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) of skin-homing CD4+ memory T lymphocytes; management is stage-adapted, employing skin-directed therapies (topical corticosteroids, nitrogen mustard, phototherapy) for early-stage disease and targeted systemic therapies (brentuximab vedotin, mogamulizumab) for advanced disease.

teaching_points.claim: The ISCL/EORTC staging system classifies MF and SS by TNMB criteria, defining Sézary syndrome as leukemic CTCL characterized by generalized erythroderma (T4) and significant peripheral blood involvement (B2: absolute Sézary cell count >=1.0 x 10^9/L, CD4/CD8 ratio >=10, or loss of CD7/CD26 on CD4+ cells).

EORTC and WHO guidelines establish that early-stage disease (Stage IA-IIA: patches and plaques covering <10% to >=10% body surface area without tumors) is managed conservatively with skin-directed therapies (topical corticosteroids, topical chlormethine/mechlorethamine gel, PUVA or narrow-band UVB phototherapy) to avoid unnecessary systemic chemotherapy toxicity.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the randomized phase 3 ALCANZA trial, the CD30-directed antibody-drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin demonstrated significant superiority over physician's choice (methotrexate or bexarotene) in CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, achieving an objective response lasting >=4 months (ORR4) of 56.3% versus 12.5% (p<0.0001).

The phase 3 MAVORIC trial showed that mogamulizumab (monoclonal antibody targeting CC chemokine receptor 4, CCR4) significantly doubled median progression-free survival compared to vorinostat (7.7 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.53; p<0.0001), demonstrating particularly high activity in the blood compartment of Sézary syndrome.

uncertainties: Timing and conditioning regimens for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation in advanced refractory Sézary syndrome.
Long-term management of mogamulizumab-associated severe autoimmune rash mimicking disease progression.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic definition of Sézary syndrome triad: generalized erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating clonally identical Sézary cells (cerebriform nuclei).
Flow cytometry signature of Sézary cells: CD4+ T cells with aberrant loss of CD7 and CD26, and CD4/CD8 ratio >=10.
ALCANZA trial outcome: brentuximab vedotin significantly superior for CD30-expressing CTCL.
First-line treatment approach for Stage IA-IB patch/plaque mycosis fungoides: skin-directed therapy (topical steroids, phototherapy, mechlorethamine gel) rather than systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy.

topic: Myelodysplastic syndrome: azacitidine hypomethylating therapy

page.mentor_intro: Azacitidine is a DNA methyltransferase inhibitor that represents the established standard-of-care hypomethylating therapy for higher-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), demonstrating proven overall survival prolongation and delayed progression to acute myeloid leukemia.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark randomized phase 3 AZA-001 trial by Fenaux and colleagues, azacitidine (75 mg/m2/day subcutaneously for 7 consecutive days every 28 days) significantly prolonged median overall survival from 15.0 months with conventional care to 24.5 months (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.43-0.77; p=0.0001) in higher-risk MDS.

In AZA-001, azacitidine almost doubled the 2-year overall survival rate compared to conventional care regimens (50.8% vs 26.2%; p<0.0001) and significantly delayed the median time to acute myeloid leukemia transformation from 11.5 to 17.8 months.

standard_knowledge.claim: Risk stratification is guided by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R), incorporating cytogenetic risk categories, marrow blast percentage, depth of cytopenias, and age; higher-risk categories (intermediate, high, very high) are standard indications for hypomethylating therapy.

European LeukemiaNet (ELN) guidelines emphasize that a minimum of 4 to 6 cycles of azacitidine must be administered before evaluating for clinical response or declaring treatment failure, as responses develop gradually over multiple treatment cycles.

uncertainties: Addition of venetoclax to azacitidine in newly diagnosed higher-risk MDS (balancing enhanced response rates against severe prolonged myelosuppression).
Optimal timing and conditioning for allogeneic stem cell transplantation in older fit patients responding to initial azacitidine cycles.
mcq_angles: Primary endpoint and landmark survival finding of AZA-001: 9.5-month median overall survival advantage and doubling of 2-year survival with azacitidine over conventional care.
Standard administration schedule of azacitidine: 75 mg/m2/day subcutaneously for 7 days every 28 days.
Crucial management rule: maintain therapy for at least 4 to 6 cycles before determining therapeutic failure.
Mechanism of action: DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibition leading to DNA hypomethylation and re-expression of silenced tumor suppressor genes.

topic: Myelodysplastic Syndromes

page.mentor_intro: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) encompass a heterogeneous spectrum of clonal hematopoietic stem cell neoplasms characterized by peripheral cytopenias, ineffective hematopoiesis, and risk of acute myeloid leukemia transformation, managed by genomic risk-stratified therapy.

teaching_points.claim: In patients with lower-risk MDS and isolated del(5q) cytogenetic abnormality, lenalidomide produces rapid and durable transfusion independence in 67% of patients and complete cytogenetic remission in 45% by targeting casein kinase 1A1 (CK1A1) for ubiquitination and degradation.

Prognostication has advanced from the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) to the Molecular IPSS (IPSS-M), which incorporates targeted next-generation sequencing across 31 genes, identifying multi-hit TP53, SF3B1, and ASXL1 as critical independent molecular risk modifiers.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the phase 3 MEDALIST trial by Fenaux and colleagues, the erythroid maturation agent luspatercept (1.0-1.75 mg/kg subcutaneously every 3 weeks) significantly reduced transfusion burden in lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts, achieving transfusion independence for >=8 weeks in 38% vs 13% with placebo (p<0.001).

For symptomatic lower-risk non-del(5q) MDS with serum erythropoietin <500 U/L and low transfusion burden, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (recombinant human EPO or darbepoetin alfa) achieve an erythroid hematologic response in 40-60% of patients.

uncertainties: Clinical threshold and sequencing of luspatercept versus erythropoietin-stimulating agents in frontline lower-risk non-mutated SF3B1 MDS.
Impact of multi-hit TP53 allelic status on post-allogeneic stem cell transplant conditioning regimens and maintenance strategies.

Specific targeted agent for lower-risk MDS with isolated del(5q): lenalidomide.

Distinction between multi-hit TP53 (biallelic mutation/deletion, conferring dismal prognosis) and monoallelic TP53.

topic: Myelofibrosis: JAK inhibition with ruxolitinib

page.mentor_intro: Myelofibrosis is a BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by dysregulated JAK-STAT signaling, causing debilitating constitutional symptoms, progressive extramedullary hematopoiesis with massive splenomegaly, and bone marrow reticulin fibrosis, effectively palliated by the oral JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib.

teaching_points.claim: In the double-blind, randomized COMFORT-I trial, ruxolitinib significantly reduced splenomegaly in primary or secondary myelofibrosis, with 41.9% of patients achieving >=35% spleen volume reduction at 24 weeks compared to 0.7% with placebo (p<0.001), accompanied by dramatic improvements in disease-related constitutional symptoms.

standard_knowledge.claim: The randomized COMFORT-II trial confirmed ruxolitinib superiority over best available therapy (28% vs 0% achieving >=35% spleen volume reduction at week 48; p<0.001) and established significant quality-of-life and functional capacity improvements.

Pooled 5-year long-term survival analyses of COMFORT-I and COMFORT-II demonstrated that ruxolitinib conferred a statistically significant 30% reduction in the risk of all-cause death (HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.54-0.91; p=0.0065) compared with control cohorts.

Ruxolitinib dosing is titrated based on baseline platelet count (20 mg twice daily for platelets >200 x 10^9/L, 15 mg twice daily for 100-200 x 10^9/L, 5 mg twice daily for 50-100 x 10^9/L); early dose-dependent anemia and thrombocytopenia represent expected mechanism-based pharmacodynamic effects rather than drug toxicity.

topic: myocardial infarction

page.mentor_intro: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is defined by the Fourth Universal Definition as cardiomyocyte necrosis in a clinical setting consistent with acute myocardial ischemia, mandating rapid differentiation between atherothrombotic plaque disruption (Type 1 MI) and supply-demand mismatch (Type 2 MI) using high-sensitivity cardiac troponin algorithms.

teaching_points.claim: ESC guidelines recommend the rapid 0h/1h or 0h/2h high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) algorithmic protocols, which achieve negative predictive values >99% for safe early discharge in the rule-out zone while rapidly identifying high-risk patients in the rule-in zone.

In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), emergency primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) is the Class I reperfusion strategy of choice if the anticipated time from STEMI diagnosis to wire crossing is <=120 minutes; otherwise, immediate intravenous fibrinolysis within 10 minutes of diagnosis is mandated.

Acute secondary prevention mandates immediate loading of dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor: ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel), high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 80 mg), and beta-blocker/ACE inhibitor initiation within 24 hours in the absence of cardiogenic shock.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Fourth Universal Definition of MI distinguishes Type 1 MI (coronary atherothrombosis caused by plaque rupture, ulceration, or erosion) from Type 2 MI (ischemic myocardial injury resulting from a mismatch between oxygen supply and demand without acute atherothrombosis, such as sustained tachyarrhythmia, severe anemia, or shock).

uncertainties: Optimal routine medical therapy versus invasive revascularization in patients with confirmed Type 2 myocardial infarction.
De-escalation of dual antiplatelet therapy from ticagrelor/prasugrel to clopidogrel or monotherapy at 1-3 months post-PCI in high bleeding risk patients.
mcq_angles: Distinction between Type 1 MI (plaque rupture/erosion) and Type 2 MI (supply/demand mismatch without thrombosis).
Maximum acceptable target delay from STEMI diagnosis to PCI wire crossing: <=120 minutes.
Superiority of ticagrelor and prasugrel over clopidogrel in acute coronary syndromes: significantly reduced ischemic events and stent thrombosis without excess overall mortality.
Definition of myocardial injury without infarction: elevated troponin without clinical, ECG, or imaging evidence of acute ischemia.

topic: Myositis-specific antibodies: anti-Jo-1, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma: clinical associations

page.mentor_intro: Myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs) delineate biologically and clinically distinct subsets of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, predicting distinct patterns of organ involvement, rapid interstitial lung disease progression, and occult malignancy risk.

topic: Narrow-complex tachycardias: SVT diagnosis, vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, ablation

page.mentor_intro: Narrow-complex tachycardia (QRS <120 ms) is a common medical emergency requiring urgent hemodynamic assessment, diagnostic 12-lead ECG appraisal of P-wave and RP relationships, physical vagal maneuvers, intravenous adenosine, and consideration of curative catheter ablation.

teaching_points.claim: In the multicenter randomized REVERT trial by Appelboam and colleagues, the modified postural Valsalva manoeuvre (straining to 40 mmHg for 15 seconds followed immediately by supine repositioning with 45-degree passive leg elevation for 15 seconds) achieved 43% cardioversion of SVT to sinus rhythm compared with only 17% for standard Valsalva (OR 3.7; NNT 3.8).

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines establish intravenous adenosine (6 mg rapid IV push through large proximal vein with saline flush, followed by 12 mg if unsuccessful) as the drug of choice for acute termination of paroxysmal SVT dependent on the AV node (AVNRT and AVRT).

Diagnostic ECG analysis categorizes regular narrow-complex tachycardias into short RP tachycardias (RP < PR interval, including typical slow-fast AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT) and long RP tachycardias (RP > PR interval, including atypical fast-slow AVNRT, permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia [PJRT], and atrial tachycardia).

Catheter ablation is the Class I definitive curative standard of care for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT and AVRT, achieving long-term success rates >97% with an exceedingly low risk of accidental permanent complete heart block (<1%).

uncertainties: Adenosine safety and alternative AV nodal blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem) in severe active asthma or bronchospasm.
Long-term stroke risk in patients undergoing successful accessory pathway ablation for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome who experience concurrent atrial fibrillation.
mcq_angles: Technique and success rate of modified Valsalva in REVERT trial: passive leg raise to 45 degrees increases cardioversion rate from 17% to 43%.
Adenosine contraindications and precautions: severe active bronchospasm, heart transplantation (extreme denervation hypersensitivity requiring reduced dose), and concurrent dipyridamole.
Differentiating regular SVT: typical AVNRT demonstrates pseudo r' in lead V1 or pseudo s' in inferior leads due to retrograde P waves embedded in terminal QRS.
Hemodynamically unstable SVT (hypotension, altered mental status, pulmonary edema): immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion.

topic: Neonatal jaundice: assessment, phototherapy and exchange transfusion

page.mentor_intro: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia affects over 60% of term and 80% of preterm infants; systematic predischarge risk assessment using transcutaneous bilirubinometry and total serum bilirubin mapped against hour-specific nomograms prevents acute bilirubin encephalopathy and irreversible kernicterus.

teaching_points.claim: The revised 2022 American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) clinical practice guideline updates hour-specific phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds, recommending universal predischarge transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) or total serum bilirubin (TSB) measurement between 24 and 48 hours of life or prior to discharge.

Bhutani and colleagues proved that plotting predischarge hour-specific bilirubin on a percentile nomogram accurately stratifies infants into risk zones (high risk >95th percentile, high intermediate, low intermediate, and low risk <40th percentile), predicting significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring readmission.

Intensive phototherapy utilizing narrow-band blue light (wavelength 460-490 nm) converts hydrophobic unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble structural photoisomers (primarily lumirubin) that are excreted directly into bile and urine without requiring hepatic glucuronidation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier when binding capacity of albumin is exceeded or in neurovascular disruption, selectively depositing in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus), subthalamic nuclei, and brainstem auditory nuclei, causing acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, hypotonia, high-pitched cry, retrocollis/opisthotonus) and chronic choreoathetoid kernicterus.

uncertainties: Use of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) in Rh or ABO hemolytic disease when total serum bilirubin approaches exchange transfusion thresholds.
Long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in late preterm infants exposed to moderate unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia without clinical encephalopathy.
mcq_angles: Phototherapy mechanism of action: structural photoisomerization of (4Z,15Z)-bilirubin into water-soluble lumirubin.
Neuroanatomical structures damaged in kernicterus: basal ganglia (globus pallidus), subthalamic nuclei, and cochlear nuclei.

Indications for exchange transfusion: failure of intensive phototherapy to reduce TSB, TSB exceeding hour-specific exchange threshold, or any clinical signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (opisthotonus, retrocollis, high-pitched cry).
Timing of universal screening: every infant must undergo TcB or TSB between 24 and 48 hours after birth.

topic: Neonatal Lupus and Congenital Heart Block

page.mentor_intro: Neonatal lupus erythematosus is an acquired autoimmune disease mediated by transplacental transfer of maternal anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB autoantibodies, causing irreversible congenital heart block (CHB) in 2% of primigravida pregnancies and carrying high fetal morbidity and pacemaker dependence.

topic: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus

page.mentor_intro: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI) results from renal collecting duct unresponsiveness to arginine vasopressin (AVP), producing massive polyuria (>3 L/24h), polydipsia, and hyposthenuria, caused congenitally by AVPR2 or AQP2 mutations or acquired through chronic lithium therapy.

teaching_points.claim: In diagnostic trials by Fenske and colleagues, plasma copeptin (the C-terminal cleavage fragment of pre-pro-vasopressin) measurement provides high accuracy: baseline un-stimulated copeptin >21.4 pmol/L confirms nephrogenic diabetes insipidus without requiring water deprivation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Congenital NDI is caused in ~90% of cases by X-linked recessive loss-of-function mutations in the arginine vasopressin type 2 receptor gene (AVPR2 on chromosome Xq28), and in ~10% by autosomal recessive or dominant mutations in the aquaporin-2 water channel gene (AQP2 on chromosome 12q13).

Chronic lithium therapy is the most common cause of acquired NDI, occurring in up to 20-40% of patients; lithium enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and accumulates intracellularly, inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase-3beta (GSK-3beta) and downregulating AQP2 gene expression.

Pharmacological management combines a low-sodium low-protein diet with a thiazide diuretic (which contracts extracellular fluid volume, increasing proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption) and amiloride (which specifically blocks ENaC, preventing further lithium uptake in principal cells).

uncertainties: Reversibility of lithium-induced NDI and chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis after long-term exposure exceeding 15 years.
Efficacy of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (indomethacin) in mitigating polyuria while monitoring for acute glomerular filtration reduction.
mcq_angles: Mechanism of lithium entry into collecting duct principal cells: via the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), which is blocked specifically by amiloride.
Inheritance and genes in congenital NDI: X-linked recessive AVPR2 in 90% (boys), autosomal recessive AQP2 in 10%.
Copeptin diagnostic cutoff: baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L confirms nephrogenic DI (high circulating vasopressin with renal resistance).
Paradoxical effect of thiazide diuretics: volume contraction reduces distal delivery of water, reducing urine output.

topic: Nephrolithiasis: Calcium Stones

page.mentor_intro: Calcium nephrolithiasis (calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate) accounts for >80% of urinary calculi; recurrence prevention is guided by 24-hour urine metabolic profiling, dietary calcium normalization, and targeted pharmacological therapies (thiazides, potassium citrate).

teaching_points.claim: Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide 25-50 mg daily, chlorthalidone 25-50 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily) stimulate renal proximal and distal tubular calcium reabsorption, significantly reducing 24-hour urinary calcium excretion and recurrent stone episodes.

standard_knowledge.claim: In a landmark 5-year randomized trial by Borghi and colleagues, a diet with normal calcium (1200 mg daily), low animal protein, and low sodium significantly reduced 5-year stone recurrence by 51% (relative risk 0.49; p=0.04) compared with a low-calcium diet (400 mg daily), because dietary calcium binds intestinal oxalate and reduces urinary oxalate excretion.

AUA and EAU guidelines recommend a 24-hour urine metabolic evaluation in high-risk or recurrent stone formers (volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, pH) to direct prevention.

Potassium citrate supplementation (30-60 mEq daily) is the primary therapy for hypocitraturia (<320 mg/day), providing alkali to increase urinary citrate excretion (a potent endogenous inhibitor of calcium stone crystallization) and alkalinize urine.

uncertainties: Cardiovascular safety and efficacy of high-dose vs low-dose thiazides in light of the NOSTONE trial.
Long-term stone recurrence prevention with plant-based diets high in oxalates (spinach, nuts) but rich in phytate and potassium.

Role of potassium citrate: treats hypocitraturia and inhibits calcium crystallization.
Thiazide mechanism in hypercalciuria: enhances distal calcium reabsorption and reduces urinary calcium excretion.

topic: Neurocritical care: management of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage

page.mentor_intro: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (aSAH) is a critical neurological emergency requiring emergent non-contrast head CT, early aneurysm securement (<24h), enteral nimodipine neuroprotection, and proactive surveillance for delayed cerebral ischemia.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial (ISAT) of 2,143 patients, endovascular coiling of ruptured intracranial aneurysms amenable to both techniques produced significantly higher 1-year independent survival (23.5% dependent/dead vs 30.9% with surgical clipping; absolute risk reduction 7.4%; p=0.0001).

topic: Neuroendocrine tumours: WHO grading G1/G2/G3, Ki-67, somatostatin receptor imaging

page.mentor_intro: Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) are classified by the WHO 2022 framework into well-differentiated tumors (G1, G2, G3) based on mitotic count and Ki-67 proliferation index; functional imaging with somatostatin receptor PET-CT directs targeted somatostatin analogues and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT).

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark phase 3 NETTER-1 trial, 177Lu-dotatate peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) combined with octreotide LAR in patients with advanced progressive midgut NETs significantly reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 79% (HR 0.21; p<0.001) compared with high-dose octreotide LAR alone.

standard_knowledge.claim: The WHO 2022 classification stratifies well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) strictly by Ki-67 proliferation index: Grade 1 (Ki-67 <3%), Grade 2 (Ki-67 3% to 20%), and Grade 3 (Ki-67 >20%), differentiating well-differentiated G3 NETs (preserved DAXX/ATRX, intact RB1/TP53) from poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas (NEC: small cell or large cell, TP53/RB1 mutated).

Somatostatin receptor PET (68Ga-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC or 64Cu-DOTATATE) has high sensitivity and specificity (about 90% or more) and outperforms octreotide scintigraphy and CT for detecting primary and metastatic NETs.

ESMO guidelines establish long-acting somatostatin analogues (octreotide LAR 30 mg or lanreotide autogel 120 mg every 4 weeks) as first-line antiproliferative and antisecretory therapy for advanced, unresectable, well-differentiated G1/G2 gastrointestinal and pancreatic NETs.

topic: Neuromuscular blocking agents in the ICU: indications and monitoring

page.mentor_intro: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) in the intensive care unit improve chest wall compliance and eliminate patient-ventilator dyssynchrony in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), requiring structured indications, deep sedation, and quantitative peripheral nerve train-of-four monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark ACURASYS trial by Papazian and colleagues, early continuous infusion of the non-depolarizing NMBA cisatracurium for 48 hours in severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) significantly improved 90-day survival (adjusted HR 0.68; p=0.04) and increased ventilator-free days.

Conversely, the large multicenter ROSE trial evaluated early neuromuscular blockade combined with modern high PEEP lung-protective ventilation and deep sedation, finding no significant difference in 90-day mortality (42.5% vs 42.8%) compared with light sedation and neuromuscular blockade used only as rescue.

standard_knowledge.claim: Continuous neuromuscular blockade is reserved for severe ARDS with refractory hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 below 150, though the ROSE trial found no mortality benefit), severe ventilator dyssynchrony, or shivering during targeted temperature management.

topic: Neuromuscular Respiratory Failure

page.mentor_intro: Neuromuscular respiratory failure results from diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle pump exhaustion in conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and myasthenic crisis, demanding serial bedside spirometry and early elective endotracheal intubation before hypercapnic arrest occurs.

teaching_points.claim: The clinical '20/30/40 rule' validated by Lawn and colleagues identifies impending ventilatory failure in Guillain-Barré syndrome and myasthenia gravis: forced vital capacity (FVC) <20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP/NIF) less negative than -30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) <40 cmH2O mandates ICU admission and elective intubation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases are dangerously insensitive late indicators; normal oxygen saturation is maintained until hypercapnic respiratory arrest is imminent, making serial upright and supine vital capacity the essential bedside monitoring tool.

Diaphragmatic weakness is clinically signaled by paradoxical abdominal inward movement during inspiration in the supine position and an acute drop in forced vital capacity >20% when moving from an upright sitting to a supine position.

In acute myasthenic crisis, immediate definitive disease-modifying therapy consists of therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days); acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) should be temporarily discontinued in intubated patients to avoid excessive tracheobronchial secretions.

uncertainties: Use of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP) as a bridge in mild neuromuscular weakness versus the risk of sudden aspiration and emergency crash intubation.
Long-term diaphragmatic pacing protocols in chronic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
mcq_angles: The 20/30/40 rule thresholds: FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP/NIF less negative than -30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O.
Single breath count test: an inability to count aloud past 15-20 on a single breath correlates with vital capacity <1 L.
Dangerous pitfall of relying on pulse oximetry: hypoxemia is a very late sign that occurs only when the patient is exhausted and in extremis.
Temporary cessation of pyridostigmine during mechanical ventilation: reduces airway secretions and avoids cholinergic crisis confusion.

topic: neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder biologic therapy

page.mentor_intro: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a severe autoimmune astrocytopathy mediated by pathogenic autoantibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG); modern targeted biologics (eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab) dramatically suppress attacks and prevent cumulative disability.

teaching_points.claim: In the randomized phase 3 PREVENT trial by Pittock and colleagues, terminal complement C5 inhibition with intravenous eculizumab reduced the adjudicated relapse rate by 94% (HR 0.06; 95% CI 0.02-0.20; p<0.001) in AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD.

standard_knowledge.claim: The phase 3 SAkuraSky trial demonstrated that the subcutaneous IL-6 receptor antagonist satralizumab added to baseline immunosuppression significantly reduced the risk of relapse by 62% overall (HR 0.38) and by 79% in AQP4-IgG-seropositive patients (HR 0.21; p=0.001).
In N-MOmentum, inebilizumab (anti-CD19) reduced the risk of an NMOSD attack by about 77% (HR 0.23) in AQP4-IgG-positive patients and reduced disability worsening.

Traditional multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies (interferon-beta, fingolimod, natalizumab) are ineffective and can trigger catastrophic relapses in NMOSD, underscoring the critical requirement for early AQP4-IgG serological testing.

uncertainties: Direct head-to-head comparison between anti-complement (eculizumab/ravulizumab), anti-IL-6R (satralizumab), and anti-CD19 (inebilizumab) strategies.
Long-term management of hypogammaglobulinemia and encapsulated bacterial infections during decades of continuous biologic maintenance.

topic: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD): AQP4-IgG, long extensive transverse myelitis

page.mentor_intro: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune demyelinating central nervous system astrocytopathy driven by complement-activating autoantibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4), classically presenting with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM), severe optic neuritis, and area postrema syndrome.

teaching_points.claim: Lennon and colleagues demonstrated that NMO-IgG autoantibodies selectively target the aquaporin-4 water channel localized on astrocytic foot processes at the blood-brain barrier, triggering complement activation, astrocyte lysis, secondary oligodendrocyte death, and severe necrotic demyelination.

standard_knowledge.claim: According to the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis (IPND) criteria, NMOSD with AQP4-IgG requires at least 1 core clinical characteristic: optic neuritis, acute myelitis (LETM), area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups, nausea, vomiting), acute brainstem syndrome, narcolepsy/diencephalic syndrome, or symptomatic cerebral syndrome.
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, a contiguous T2 cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments, is a characteristic MRI feature of NMOSD, typically central with cord swelling.

Area postrema syndrome (intractable nausea, vomiting or hiccups for 48 hours or more without another cause) occurs in about one in ten presentations and reflects AQP4-IgG-mediated inflammation of the dorsal medulla.

Optimal acute rescue therapy: immediate concurrent plasma exchange alongside IV pulse methylprednisolone versus sequential therapy.

topic: neuropathic leg ulcer

page.mentor_intro: Neuropathic leg and foot ulcers result from sensorimotor and autonomic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, characterized by painless ulceration over high-pressure plantar prominences, requiring structured offloading (total contact casting), sharp surgical debridement, and osteomyelitis exclusion.

teaching_points.claim: The probe-to-bone (PTB) test is an essential clinical assessment: in a prospective validation by Grayson and colleagues, palpating hard gritty bone with a sterile metallic probe in an infected ulcer had a positive predictive value of 89% for underlying osteomyelitis, guiding the requirement for plain radiography, MRI, or bone biopsy.

standard_knowledge.claim: According to the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) guidelines, loss of protective sensation (LOPS) confirmed by an inability to feel the 10-gram Semmes-Weinstein monofilament on plantar surfaces is the primary predisposing cause of neuropathic foot ulceration.

IWGDF guidelines establish non-removable knee-high offloading devices (total contact cast [TCC] or non-removable knee-high walker) as the first-choice standard of care for healing plantar neuropathic forefoot and midfoot ulcers, significantly accelerating healing rates compared to removable therapeutic shoes.

Autonomic neuropathy contributes to ulcer pathogenesis through anhidrosis (causing dry, cracked, hyperkeratotic fissures) and sympathetic denervation, opening arteriovenous shunts that produce bounding foot pulses in warm, insensate, high-risk feet.

uncertainties: Antibiotic therapy duration (6 weeks vs 3 weeks) in diabetic foot osteomyelitis treated without bone resection.
Long-term ulcer recurrence prevention comparing patient-administered home dermal infrared temperature monitoring against routine nurse visits.
mcq_angles: Primary intervention with highest evidence for healing plantar neuropathic ulcers: non-removable knee-high total contact casting.
Significance of a positive probe-to-bone test: high positive predictive value (~89%) for underlying osteomyelitis in high-prevalence settings.
Clinical test confirming loss of protective sensation: 10-gram Semmes-Weinstein monofilament.

Anatomical location of pure neuropathic vs ischemic ulcers: neuropathic ulcers occur on weight-bearing plantar surfaces (metatarsal heads, heels); ischemic ulcers occur on distal digits and lateral borders of the foot.

topic: Neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy

page.mentor_intro: Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, characterized by spontaneous burning pain, hyperalgesia, and allodynia, treated according to evidence-based consensus guidelines prioritizing gabapentinoids, SNRIs, and tricyclic antidepressants while strictly limiting opioids.

teaching_points.claim: In the NeuPSIG / International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) systematic review and meta-analysis by Finnerup and colleagues, three drug classes were established as first-line Level A evidence for neuropathic pain: gabapentinoids (pregabalin, gabapentin), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (duloxetine, venlafaxine), and tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline).

Gabapentinoids (pregabalin 150-600 mg daily, gabapentin 900-3600 mg daily) bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing presynaptic excitatory neurotransmitter release with a number needed to treat (NNT) of approximately 7.2 for >=50% pain reduction.

Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline 10-75 mg at bedtime) exhibit the lowest NNT (~3.6) across peripheral neuropathic pain conditions, but carry significant anticholinergic adverse effects, sedation, and cardiotoxicity (QTc prolongation, fatal ventricular arrhythmias in overdose) requiring baseline ECG screening.

standard_knowledge.claim: Duloxetine (60 to 120 mg daily) inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, enhancing descending inhibition, with proven efficacy in painful diabetic neuropathy (NNT about 5 to 6) and fewer anticholinergic effects than tricyclics.

uncertainties: Safety and efficacy of combination pharmacotherapy (e.g., gabapentin plus duloxetine) versus sequential high-dose monotherapy.
Long-term dependency, tolerance, and misuse potential of gabapentinoids in patients with comorbid substance use disorders.
mcq_angles: First-line drug classes recommended by IASP/NeuPSIG guidelines: gabapentinoids (pregabalin/gabapentin), SNRIs (duloxetine), and TCAs (amitriptyline).
Target of gabapentin and pregabalin: alpha-2-delta (alpha2delta) subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels.
Strong recommendation against opioids (tramadol, oxycodone, morphine) as first-line therapy due to high abuse liability, hyperalgesia, and lack of long-term functional efficacy.
First-line topical alternative for localized peripheral neuropathic pain (e.g., post-herpetic neuralgia): 5% lidocaine plaster or 8% capsaicin patch.

topic: new airway devices

page.mentor_intro: Airway management in emergency and critical care settings has evolved with modern video laryngoscopes, second-generation supraglottic airway devices, and rigid bougies, which significantly enhance first-pass intubation success and reduce hypoxemic and aspiration complications.

teaching_points.claim: In the randomized BOUGIE trial by Driver and colleagues, using an endotracheal tube introducer (bougie) on the first attempt significantly increased first-pass intubation success (98% vs 87%; p<0.001) compared with an endotracheal tube with stylet in patients with anticipated difficult airways.

Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines mandate that second-generation supraglottic airway devices (SADs, such as i-gel and LMA Supreme) are the rescue devices of choice for 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) scenarios; their gastric drainage channels isolate the airway and protect against pulmonary aspiration.

The Fourth National Audit Project (NAP4) identified that failure to use capnography was a major contributing factor in over 70% of ICU and emergency airway-related deaths, establishing continuous waveform capnography as a non-negotiable mandatory standard for all tracheal intubations.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the DEVICE trial of 1,417 critically ill adults, video laryngoscopy increased first-pass intubation success (85.1% versus 70.8%, about a 14 percentage point gain) compared with direct laryngoscopy.

topic: New-onset seizure in adults: diagnostic workup, EEG patterns, imaging

page.mentor_intro: A new-onset unprovoked seizure in an adult requires emergency exclusion of acute metabolic, toxic, or structural etiologies, followed by dedicated neuroimaging, electroencephalography, and recurrence risk stratification to guide anti-seizure medication (ASM) initiation under the ILAE 2014 definition of epilepsy.

teaching_points.claim: AAN and AES guidelines state that unprovoked first seizure recurrence risk is highest in the first 2 years (21-45%); immediate initiation of anti-seizure medication reduces 2-year recurrence risk by approximately 35% compared to deferred therapy, although it does not alter long-term remission rates.

standard_knowledge.claim: According to the ILAE official definition, epilepsy is diagnosed after a single unprovoked seizure if the individual has an enduring predisposition to further seizures, defined as an estimated recurrence risk >=60% over the next 10 years (e.g., significant epileptogenic structural MRI lesion or clear epileptiform discharges on EEG).

In the SANAD II multicenter randomized trial, lamotrigine was superior to levetiracetam and zonisamide as first-line monotherapy for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, demonstrating significantly higher treatment success (12-month remission) and superior cost-effectiveness.

Neuroimaging standards require high-resolution brain MRI utilizing an epilepsy-dedicated protocol (including 3D volumetric T1, T2 perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, and 3D fluid-attenuated inversion recovery [FLAIR]) to detect subtle cortical dysplasias, mesial temporal sclerosis, or low-grade neoplasms.

uncertainties: Prognostic significance of routine 30-minute EEG versus 24-hour ambulatory EEG in unprovoked first seizures with normal initial brain MRI.

topic: Nitrate therapy: GTN, isosorbide mononitrate, tolerance, combination use

page.mentor_intro: Organic nitrates (glyceryl trinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate, isosorbide dinitrate) provide venodilation, reduce myocardial preload and coronary vasospasm, but develop rapid tolerance requiring an asymmetric 10-14 hour nitrate-free interval, and are strictly contraindicated with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: ESC guidelines recommend short-acting sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN tablet or spray) as first-line Class I therapy for immediate relief of acute angina symptoms and pre-effort prophylaxis, while oral long-acting nitrates are secondary add-on anti-anginal agents when beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers are insufficient or contraindicated.

standard_knowledge.claim: In a randomized clinical trial by Parker and colleagues, continuous round-the-clock administration of nitrates induced complete loss of anti-anginal and hemodynamic efficacy within 24-48 hours (nitrate tolerance), which was prevented by an asymmetric eccentric dosing schedule (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate at 08:00 and 15:00) providing a 10-14 hour daily nitrate-free interval.

Molecular mechanisms of nitrate tolerance involve depletion of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH-2, which bioactivates nitroglycerin), uncoupling of endothelial nitric oxide synthase, increased reactive oxygen species generation, and neurohormonal activation.

Co-administration of organic nitrates with phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) causes synergistic accumulation of cyclic GMP, resulting in catastrophic, refractory, life-threatening hypotension and myocardial infarction; nitrates must be withheld for >=24 hours after sildenafil/vardenafil and >=48 hours after tadalafil.

uncertainties: Rebound angina and nocturnal ischemic risk occurring during the mandatory nitrate-free interval in severe multivessel coronary artery disease.
Long-term cardiovascular outcome impact of hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate in non-Black HFrEF cohorts.
mcq_angles: Method to prevent nitrate tolerance: asymmetric dosing schedule providing a daily 10-14 hour nitrate-free interval.
Contraindication with PDE-5 inhibitors: absolute prohibition within 24 hours of sildenafil/vardenafil and 48 hours of tadalafil.
Primary enzyme responsible for bioactivation of nitroglycerin into nitric oxide: mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH-2).
Hemodynamic mechanism of anti-anginal action: venodilation causing reduced venous return and decreased left ventricular end-diastolic wall tension (preload reduction).

topic: Renovascular Disease and Renal Artery Stenosis

topic: Secondary adrenal insufficiency: HPA axis testing, glucocorticoid replacement, sick day rules

page.mentor_intro: Secondary adrenal insufficiency results from ACTH deficiency, with mineralocorticoid function preserved. Diagnosis uses the synacthen test and pituitary evaluation, and patients need sick day rules.

standard_knowledge.claim: Secondary adrenal insufficiency is characterized by deficient ACTH secretion with preserved mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) synthesis because the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis remains intact; fludrocortisone replacement is not required.

page.mentor_intro: STEMI diagnosis requires distinguishing mimics (pericarditis, early repolarisation, LVH) and recognising occlusion in LBBB or paced rhythm with the modified Sgarbossa criteria; reperfusion is time-critical.

teaching_points.claim: Important electrocardiographic mimics of STEMI include acute pericarditis (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR segment depression), benign early repolarization, left ventricular hypertrophy (voltage criteria with strain pattern), and Brugada syndrome.

In patients with left bundle branch block (LBBB) or ventricular paced rhythm, modified Sgarbossa criteria identify acute coronary occlusion: concordant ST elevation >=1 mm, concordant ST depression >=1 mm in V1-V3, or excessively discordant ST elevation/S-wave ratio <= -0.25.

Emergent coronary angiography is indicated in patients with resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and ST elevation on ECG, or in patients with hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, or persistent ischemic chest pain despite equivocal ECG findings.

topic: TB treatment: RIPE regimen, hepatotoxicity monitoring, directly observed therapy, drug-resistant TB

page.mentor_intro: Drug-susceptible tuberculosis is treated with 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol then 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid. Liver injury, neuropathy prevention and observed therapy are key.

standard_knowledge.claim: Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis comprises a 2-month intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (RI).

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) requires withholding hepatotoxic drugs (pyrazinamide > isoniazid > rifampicin) if serum transaminases exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal (or 3 times ULN with symptoms of jaundice, nausea, or abdominal pain).

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) is routinely co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in patients with diabetes, alcohol dependence, renal failure, malnutrition, or pregnancy.

topic: Thyroid storm: Burch-Wartofsky score, propylthiouracil, beta-blockade, supportive care

page.mentor_intro: Thyroid storm is diagnosed with the Burch-Wartofsky score and treated with antithyroid drug, iodine after thionamide, beta-blockade, steroids and supportive care.

teaching_points.claim: The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS score >=45 highly suggestive) quantifies end-organ dysfunction (thermoregulatory, CNS agitation/coma, cardiovascular tachyarrhythmias, heart failure, and GI-hepatic dysfunction) to establish clinical diagnosis without awaiting lab confirmation.

Multimodal medical therapy follows a strict sequence: (1) high-dose antithyroid drug (propylthiouracil 200 mg every 4 hours preferred over methimazole due to inhibition of peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); (2) inorganic iodine (Lugols solution or SSKI) administered at least 1 hour AFTER antithyroid drugs to block thyroid hormone release without providing substrate; (3) beta-blockers (propranolol); and (4) intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours) to prevent adrenal crisis and inhibit peripheral deiodination.

Supportive management includes aggressive active cooling (avoiding aspirin, which displaces thyroid hormone from binding globulins), broad-spectrum treatment of underlying precipitating triggers (sepsis, surgery, DKA), and bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) to disrupt enterohepatic hormone recirculation.

topic: Typhoid fever: Salmonella typhi, Widal test, blood culture, azithromycin, ceftriaxone

page.mentor_intro: Enteric fever causes step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia and rose spots, with perforation a feared third-week complication.

teaching_points.claim: Enteric (typhoid) fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi presents with step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), rose spots, and hepatosplenomegaly; blood culture is the definitive diagnostic gold standard (Widal test is unreliable due to high false-positive and false-negative rates); empirical first-line treatment for travelers returning from endemic areas (South Asia) is intravenous ceftriaxone or high-dose oral azithromycin due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance.

standard_knowledge.claim: Intestinal perforation occurs in 1-3% of hospitalized typhoid fever cases, classically during the third week of illness due to necrosis of Peyer patches in the terminal ileum, requiring emergent surgical laparotomy and expanded broad-spectrum coverage.

topic: Uveitis in JIA: silent inflammation, slit-lamp screening, methotrexate, adalimumab

page.mentor_intro: JIA-associated uveitis is silent, so regular slit-lamp screening is essential; treatment escalates from topical steroids to methotrexate and adalimumab.

standard_knowledge.claim: JIA-associated uveitis is typically asymptomatic ('white eye'), so regular slit-lamp screening (about every 3 months in high-risk children: oligoarticular or polyarticular, ANA-positive, onset under 7 years) is recommended.

Topical corticosteroids are first-line for active anterior uveitis; however, disease requiring more than 1-2 drops daily after 3 months warrants initiation of subcutaneous methotrexate to prevent band keratopathy, cataracts, glaucoma, and vision loss.
In methotrexate-refractory or intolerant JIA-associated uveitis, the monoclonal TNF antibody adalimumab (supported by the landmark SYCAMORE trial) is the evidence-based first-line biologic.

topic: Vaccinations in immunosuppressed rheumatology patients: timing, live vs killed, pneumococcal, shingles

page.mentor_intro: Immunosuppressed rheumatology patients should receive inactivated vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster) and avoid live vaccines.

topic: Varicella zoster in adults and immunocompromised: severity, aciclovir, VZIG prophylaxis

page.mentor_intro: Varicella in adults and the immunocompromised can cause pneumonia, hepatitis and encephalitis; treat with intravenous aciclovir and consider VZIG for susceptible exposed patients.

topic: Vasopressor and inotrope pharmacology: noradrenaline, vasopressin, dobutamine, milrinone

page.mentor_intro: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in shock; vasopressin is a second agent, dobutamine and milrinone provide inotropy, and adrenaline is added in refractory shock.

teaching_points.claim: Noradrenaline (potent alpha-1 with modest beta-1 agonist activity) is the evidence-based first-line vasopressor in septic and vasodilatory shock to restore vascular tone and target mean arterial pressure >=65 mmHg; vasopressin (pure V1a receptor agonist) is added as a second-line sparing agent to reduce noradrenaline requirements, while dobutamine (beta-1 inotrope) is added for persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP in cardiogenic dysfunction.

standard_knowledge.claim: Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that raises cAMP, giving inotropy and systemic and pulmonary vasodilation (an 'inodilator'); hypotension and arrhythmia limit use, and it is useful in cardiogenic shock with raised pulmonary vascular resistance.
Adrenaline (epinephrine) is added as an adjunct or alternative in refractory shock, but can induce transient lactic acidosis due to accelerated aerobic glycolysis via beta-2 receptor stimulation.

topic: Viral hepatitis A and E: faeco-oral transmission, self-limiting, vaccination, fulminant hepatitis

page.mentor_intro: Hepatitis A and E are faeco-orally transmitted, usually self-limiting, but hepatitis E is dangerous in pregnancy and can become chronic in transplant recipients.

standard_knowledge.claim: Hepatitis A (HAV) and Hepatitis E (HEV genotypes 1 and 2) are transmitted primarily via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food and water, causing acute self-limiting hepatitis diagnosed by serum IgM antibodies.
Hepatitis E infection during pregnancy (especially in the third trimester with genotypes 1 and 2) carries a devastating risk of fulminant hepatic failure and maternal mortality approaching 20-25%.

In solid organ transplant recipients and immunosuppressed individuals, HEV (genotype 3) can cause chronic hepatitis and rapid progression to cirrhosis, requiring reduction in immunosuppression and treatment with oral ribavirin.

topic: viral wheeze

page.mentor_intro: Viral wheeze in preschool children is triggered by respiratory viruses and treated with short-acting bronchodilators for episodes; preventive treatment depends on frequency and severity.

teaching_points.claim: In preschool children, viral-induced wheeze is primarily triggered by common respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, RSV) without atopic sensitization; acute treatment centers on inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol via metered-dose inhaler with spacer) titrated to clinical response, whereas routine oral corticosteroids are not recommended in mild-to-moderate preschool viral wheeze due to clear evidence of lack of clinical efficacy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In selected preschool children with episodic viral wheeze, short courses of high-dose inhaled corticosteroid started at the onset of respiratory infection have reduced exacerbations in some trials, but this approach is not routine and raises growth concerns; oral steroids or montelukast are alternatives.

topic: vitamin K antagonist bridging atrial fibrillation perioperative BRIDGE trial

page.mentor_intro: Perioperative bridging with heparin is not needed for most patients with atrial fibrillation on warfarin (BRIDGE trial) but remains recommended for mechanical valves at high thrombotic risk.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark BRIDGE randomized trial of patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation receiving warfarin who required temporary interruption for elective procedures, bridging anticoagulation with therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) failed to reduce arterial thromboembolism (0.4% vs 0.3%) and significantly tripled the risk of major bleeding (3.2% vs 1.3%) compared with no bridging, establishing that routine heparin bridging is unnecessary and harmful for standard-risk AF.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients with mechanical heart valves, particularly in the mitral position or with older-generation valves, therapeutic LMWH or unfractionated heparin bridging remains recommended perioperatively despite the findings of the BRIDGE trial in non-valvular AF.

topic: V/Q Mismatch and pulmonary gas exchange

page.mentor_intro: V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia and corrects with supplemental oxygen; shunt does not, and dead space impairs carbon dioxide clearance.

standard_knowledge.claim: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia in clinical medicine (e.g. COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease) and is characterized by an elevated alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient that corrects with low-to-moderate supplemental oxygen (FiO2 0.3-0.5).

True right-to-left anatomical or physiological shunt (V/Q ratio of zero, seen in severe ARDS, dense lobar consolidation, and intracardiac shunts) presents with refractory hypoxemia that does not fully correct even with 100% inspired oxygen.
Dead-space ventilation (V/Q ratio approaching infinity, seen in pulmonary embolism) impairs carbon dioxide elimination, resulting in hypercapnia and increased minute ventilation requirements.

topic: wheeze phenotypes

page.mentor_intro: Preschool wheeze phenotypes (transient, viral, atopic persistent) guide prognosis and treatment; atopic persistent wheeze benefits from daily inhaled steroid.

teaching_points.claim: Childhood wheezing is categorized into distinct phenotypes: transient early wheeze (associated with smaller airway caliber and maternal smoking, resolving by age 3-6), non-atopic viral wheeze (triggered by viral infections, generally improving in school age), and persistent atopic wheeze/asthma (characterized by atopic sensitization, allergic rhinitis/eczema, elevated FeNO, and persistent airway hyperresponsiveness into adulthood).

standard_knowledge.claim: Preschool children with persistent atopic wheeze and airway eosinophilia benefit from daily maintenance inhaled corticosteroid, with fewer exacerbations.

topic: workup for new heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

page.mentor_intro: New heart failure with reduced ejection fraction needs echocardiography, laboratory tests including iron studies and thyroid function, and evaluation for coronary disease, followed by four-pillar drug therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Iron deficiency (ferritin <100 ug/L, or 100-299 ug/L with TSAT <20%) occurs in up to 50% of HFrEF patients; intravenous ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose improves symptoms, quality of life, and reduces heart failure hospitalizations.

Guideline-directed medical therapy with the four foundational pillar drug classes (ARNI/ACEi, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor) should be initiated and uptitrated promptly to reduce cardiovascular mortality.

standard_knowledge.claim: Comprehensive diagnostic evaluation of newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) requires comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography, laboratory evaluation (NT-proBNP, complete blood count, renal and liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone, ferritin and transferrin saturation to detect iron deficiency), and non-invasive or invasive coronary angiography to exclude ischemic heart disease, alongside cardiac MRI when non-ischemic cardiomyopathy or myocarditis is suspected.
